seoTitle: How to Find 52 Week High Stocks in TradingView
metaDescription: Use TradingView's Stock Screener to find stocks near their 52-week high, apply the New High 52 weeks filter, and confirm breakouts before trading them.
intro: Finding stocks that are pushing to new yearly highs is much faster with TradingView's built-in Stock Screener than checking charts one by one. A 52-week high often signals real buying strength, and the Screener lets you surface every stock hitting one right now instead of relying on a scattered watchlist or news headlines. This guide walks through opening the Screener, applying the exact filter that isolates 52-week highs, and layering on volume and market cap so the list stays focused on stocks you can actually trade.
costNote: The Stock Screener, including the New high 52 weeks filter, works on TradingView's free Basic plan. The Basic plan does limit exporting Screener results to a file compared to paid tiers, but browsing, filtering, and sorting the table itself doesn't need a paid plan.

steps.heading: Understand what a 52-week high means
steps.body: A 52-week high is the highest price a stock has traded at over the past year. Traders watch this level because pushing through it, or trading near it, often reflects sustained buying interest instead of a one-day spike. Institutions and momentum traders both pay attention when a name breaks into new territory with no overhead resistance left from the past year of trading.

steps.heading: Open TradingView and check the watchlist first
steps.body: From TradingView's homepage you already get a live snapshot of major indices, world stocks, and your personal watchlist in the right-hand panel, with real-time price and percent-change data for whatever you're tracking (Apple, Tesla, and Netflix, in a typical setup). This isn't the Screener itself, but it's a useful gut-check before you dive into filtering: if a stock you already follow is showing a sharp green move, it's worth noting before you go looking for others doing the same thing.

image.caption: TradingView's homepage, with world indices and a live watchlist panel on the right showing real-time price and percentage change for AAPL, TSLA, and NFLX.

steps.heading: Open the Stock Screener
steps.body: Navigate to the Stock Screener from TradingView's Products menu. The default view is "All stocks," showing your local market sorted by market cap, with a full row of filter dropdowns across the top: Watchlist, Index, Price, Change %, Market cap, P/E, EPS dil growth, Div yield %, Sector, Analyst Rating, and more, sitting above a sortable table of every stock in the market with columns for price, change, volume, relative volume, and market cap.

image.caption: The Stock Screener's default "All stocks" view, with filter dropdowns across the top and a full sortable table below.

steps.heading: Apply the New High 52 weeks filter
steps.body: Click the "+" next to the existing filter row and search for the 52-week high filter; it appears in the toolbar as "New high 52 weeks." Adding it immediately cuts the table down from thousands of stocks to only those currently at a fresh yearly high. In a real scan this pulled the list down to 910 names, including Walmart, Exxon Mobil, Johnson & Johnson, and Chevron near the top by market cap. That's still a lot to work through, which is exactly why the next filters matter.

image.caption: The Screener with the "New high 52 weeks" filter active, narrowing the results table to 910 stocks currently at a fresh yearly high.

steps.heading: Narrow further with volume, price, and market cap
steps.body: A 52-week high on thin volume is far less meaningful than one backed by real participation, so add a minimum volume or relative volume filter to cut out illiquid names. Set a price range that fits what you're willing to trade, and add a market cap filter to decide between large, liquid names or the extra volatility of small caps. Sort the remaining list by relative volume to put the stocks with unusually high trading activity at the top: those are the ones most likely reacting to real news instead of drifting up on light volume.

steps.heading: Confirm the breakout on the chart
steps.body: A Screener match is a starting point, not a trade signal on its own. Click into each shortlisted symbol and check the chart directly. Is the move backed by a volume spike? Is price holding above the old high or already fading back below it? Do the indicators you rely on, moving averages, RSI, or volume profile, support the strength the Screener flagged? This step separates a real breakout candidate from a stock that briefly poked above its old high and reversed before you saw the row.

steps.heading: Match the list to your trading style
steps.body: How you use this shortlist depends on your timeframe. Intraday traders want the names with the heaviest relative volume and tightest spreads today. Swing traders care more about a clean break with room to run before the next resistance level. Longer-term investors should weight fundamentals from the same Screener columns (P/E, EPS growth, sector) over the short-term price action, since a stock at a 52-week high can still be a poor long-term hold if the underlying business doesn't support the move.

troubleshooting.problem: The New high 52 weeks filter returns a list that still feels unfiltered
troubleshooting.cause: This filter only checks whether a stock is at a fresh yearly high. It says nothing about volume or liquidity, so illiquid names sit right next to major caps.
troubleshooting.fix: Stack a volume or relative volume filter and a market cap filter on top of it, as in the narrowing step, before treating the list as a shortlist.

troubleshooting.problem: Exporting the filtered results asks for an upgrade
troubleshooting.cause: TradingView's free Basic plan limits exporting Screener data to a file compared to paid tiers.
troubleshooting.fix: Work from the in-app table (sort and filter there) instead of exporting, or upgrade if you specifically need the file export.

troubleshooting.problem: A stock on the New High list is already fading below its old high on the chart
troubleshooting.cause: The Screener's table doesn't update tick by tick, so a fast reversal right after the high can lag behind on the list for a short stretch.
troubleshooting.fix: Always check the live chart before treating a Screener row as current; that's the point of confirming the breakout as its own step.

faq.question: Is the Stock Screener free on TradingView?
faq.answer: Yes. The Stock Screener with its core filters, including the New high 52 weeks filter, is available on TradingView's free Basic plan. Exporting the results to a file is more limited on Basic than on paid tiers.

faq.question: How do I filter specifically for 52-week highs?
faq.answer: Add the "New high 52 weeks" filter from the "+" button next to the existing filter row in the Stock Screener. It isolates stocks currently trading at a fresh yearly high.

faq.question: Why do some 52-week high stocks reverse quickly?
faq.answer: A breakout without strong volume support can fail and reverse fast, which is why confirming with volume and broader chart context on the individual stock's chart matters before treating a Screener match as a trade.

faq.question: Can I save my Screener filters for future use?
faq.answer: Yes. Click Save in the Screener toolbar to store your filter set, including the 52-week high filter plus your volume and market cap criteria, so you can reopen the same scan later.

faq.question: Should I trade every stock the Screener flags?
faq.answer: No. Treat the Screener as a shortlist generator, not a signal service. Confirm volume and price action on the individual chart, and weight the list differently depending on whether you trade intraday, swing, or long term.
